title: Structured output
objectives: ask for JSON and know it will not always obey
say why JSON.parse throws on a real reply
validate the shape and fall back when it is wrong

steps.instruction: Everything it returns is a string. Your app almost never wants a string.
body: You want an array of tags, a score, a list of steps. Things your code can loop over.
The model has one output channel: text.
So you ask for text shaped like data, and then you turn it into data.
steps.keypoint: It returns a string. Turning that into an object is your job, and it is where this breaks.

steps.instruction: You asked for JSON. What actually comes back?
steps.after: There is your JSON, wrapped in a greeting and a code fence. This is what real models do.
opts: A greeting, a code fence, and the JSON inside
steps.why: The JSON is in there and it is correct. It is just wrapped in a greeting and a markdown fence, which is exactly what breaks JSON.parse.

steps.instruction: Three ways a reply that contains valid JSON still breaks your parser.
body: The JSON is in there, every time. It is just not alone.
You asked a text machine for data and got text containing data.
steps.keypoint: The JSON is usually correct. What surrounds it is the problem.

steps.instruction: So what happens when you hand that whole reply straight to JSON.parse?
opts: It works, the JSON is valid
It throws, because the reply starts with Sure! not with a brace
steps.why: JSON.parse reads from the first character. That character is S, so it fails immediately, and it never gets as far as the perfectly good JSON further down.
steps.after: The data was fine. The wrapping killed it.
steps.keypoint: JSON.parse needs the whole string to be JSON, not to contain some.

steps.instruction: First brace to last brace, then parse.
steps.after: First brace to last brace. Crude, and it survives every one of those three failure shapes.
body: Crude, and it survives a greeting before, a fence around, and an explanation after.

steps.instruction: The prompt now says ONLY valid JSON, no fences. What comes back?
steps.after: Clean, first time. The prompt fixed what the parser was cleaning up after.
steps.why: Clean, first time. The prompt fixed what the parser was cleaning up after. Do both anyway.

steps.instruction: Do both. Ask properly, and still parse defensively.
body: The prompt makes the clean case common. It does not make the messy case impossible.
A model that obeyed a thousand times can still add a greeting on the thousand and first.
Your parser runs on every reply. It has to survive the bad one.
steps.keypoint: Ask nicely, then assume it did not listen.

steps.instruction: Which of these survives the crude first-brace-to-last-brace approach?
steps.why: The first three all contain a complete object between the first and last brace. The fourth has no braces at all, so indexOf returns -1 and the slice is nonsense. That is why you never skip the fallback.
steps.after: Three out of four is not good enough. The fourth is the one that pages you at midnight.
steps.keypoint: Every parser needs an answer for the reply that has no JSON in it at all.

body: That parsed perfectly. It is still wrong: you wanted an array of tags and got one string.
Your next line is tags.map(...) and it throws, three files away from the cause.
Check the shape before you use it, not after.
steps.keypoint: It parsed does not mean it is what you asked for.

steps.instruction: It parsed fine. tags came back as a string, not an array. What prints?
steps.after: Caught it right where it happened, instead of three files later.
steps.why: Parsing succeeded and the shape is still wrong. Without this check, the crash happens later, in a file that has nothing to do with the cause.

steps.instruction: Complete the fallback so a bad reply never throws.
steps.after: Returning undefined gives the caller something to check. Throwing gives them a crash.
steps.keypoint: Fail to a value the caller can test, not to an exception.

steps.after: Asked properly, parsed defensively, and it cannot throw. That is production shape.
body: It cannot throw. On a bad day it prints unavailable, and the page stays up.
